explanation:
## Read, then inspect

```cpp
std::vector<int> v;
long long sum{};

for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
{
    int x{};
    std::cin >> x;
    v.push_back(x);
    sum += x;
}
```

`push_back` appends and grows the vector as needed. `sum` is accumulated in the
same pass because it costs nothing to do there, and the data has to be stored
anyway for the last question.

## Why the values have to be stored at all

min, max and sum are all **streaming** quantities: each can be maintained as
the values go past, and a program that only needed those three would never need
a container at all.

`above` is different. It compares each value against the mean, and the mean is
not known until the last value has been read. So either you store the values
and make a second pass, or you read the input twice - and you cannot read stdin
twice. **That** is what the vector is for: a question whose answer depends on
all the data at once.

Recognising which of those two kinds a problem is remains useful long after
this exercise. It is the difference between a constant-memory algorithm and one
that needs the whole input, and it is why stream-processing systems make such a
fuss about windowing.

## min and max start from the data

```cpp
int lo{ v[0] };
int hi{ v[0] };
```

Not `int hi{ 0 }`. The hidden case `-5 -1 -3 -2` has a maximum of -1, and a `hi`
that starts at 0 is never replaced, so the program reports a maximum of **0** -
a number that is not in the list and never was.

Starting from a "sufficiently large" sentinel such as `99999` has the same
flavour of bug one input further out. Starting from an actual element cannot be
wrong, and it is the reason the `n <= 0` case is handled before this line -
`v[0]` on an empty vector is out of range.

## The comparison that must not use division

```cpp
if (static_cast<long long>(x) * n > sum) ++above;
```

The obvious version is wrong:

```cpp
if (x > sum / n) ++above;        // integer division truncates
```

For `3 1 4 1 5`, `sum / n` is `14 / 5` = `2`, so the test becomes `x > 2` and
counts 3, 4, 5 - which happens to be right here, by luck. The two versions only
disagree when truncation lands a value **in the gap** between the real mean and
its floor. Take `2 2 2 3`: the mean is 2.25, so only `3` is above it and the
answer is 1. The truncating version computes `9 / 4` = `2` and tests `x > 2`,
which also gives 1. Now take `2 2 3 3`: mean 2.5, answer 2 - and `10 / 4` = `2`
gives 2 as well. The gap only bites when a value equals the floor of the mean
while the mean itself is higher: `3 3 3 1` has mean 2.5, the correct answer is 3,
and `10 / 4` = `2` with `x > 2` also says 3.

Finding an input where they differ takes real effort, and that is exactly what
makes it dangerous: the wrong version passes everything you would think to try,
then differs on data you did not. Multiplying through removes the question
entirely rather than making you answer it:

```
x > sum / n        becomes        x * n > sum
```

Valid because `n > 0`, so the inequality does not flip. The same trick compares
fractions without floating point, and it is how you keep a comparison exact when
it has to be.

`static_cast<long long>` is on the product because `x * n` with two `int`s is
computed as an `int`. With `x` near two billion and `n` at 1000 that overflows,
and signed overflow is undefined behaviour - not "wraps to a negative", but "the
compiler may assume it cannot happen". Widening one operand widens the whole
multiplication.

## Floating point would also work, carefully

```cpp
double mean = static_cast<double>(sum) / n;
if (x > mean) ++above;
```

Correct for these inputs. `double` has 53 bits of mantissa, so every value and
sum here is represented exactly and the division is correctly rounded - the
comparison can only go wrong when `x` sits within one rounding step of the mean,
which needs far larger numbers than the tests use.

Integer arithmetic is still preferable: it is exact by construction rather than
exact by argument, and "I checked the mantissa is wide enough" is a worse reason
to believe a program than "there is no rounding".

## The empty case

```cpp
if (!(std::cin >> n) || n <= 0) { /* print zeros */ return 0; }
```

Zero values has a defensible answer - nothing is above the mean of nothing - and
a defined output beats a crash. The guard also protects `v[0]` below, which is
the real reason it comes first.
